catalog_quote: [p. 3, Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)] Stress is predictable and generally goes to the penultimate syllable of a word. Stress is generally realized as high pitch and lengthened vowel. Vowel length does not occur in reduplicated syllables, reduplicated syllable pairs or in syllables with two vowels. Words with reduplicated syllable pairs have two stresses – the primary on the penultimate syllable and the secondary on the first syllable of the syllable pair that is being reduplicated. ˌssˈss ˌba.giˈba.gi 'work' [p. 4] /u/ is pronounced [u] in stressed syllables and word initially, and [ʊ] in all other environments. [pp. 2-3, examples] wapa ‘plenty’ [ˈwɐpɐ] ... tululu ‘cold’ [tʊˈɺuɺʊ] ... kokoleko ‘sweet potato’ [kɔkɔˈɺɛkɔ] ... yokuyoku ‘sweat’ [ˌjɔkʊˈjɔkʊ] ... taulinemo ‘at the back’ [tɐʊɺiˈnɛmɔ]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Re-extracted with extracted text (5 pp., A4, text layer present, Doulos SIL embedded; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Microsoft Word - Kakabai OPD'). Page 3 carries the heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' followed by four bullet sentences that match the quoted passage word for word: 'Stress is predictable and generally goes to the penultimate syllable of a word.' / 'Stress is generally realized as high pitch and lengthened vowel.' / 'Vowel length does not occur in reduplicated syllables, reduplicated syllable pairs or in syllables with two vowels.' / 'Words with reduplicated syllable pairs have two stresses – the primary on the penultimate syllable and the secondary on the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and falls on the penultimate syllable, cued by high pitch and vowel lengthening; in full-reduplicated forms primary stress stays on the penult and a secondary stress falls on the first syllable of the reduplicated pair (initial syllable of the base). Example transcriptions on pp. 2-3 mark penultimate stress throughout (e.g. [ˈwɐpɐ] 'plenty', [tʊˈɺuɺʊ] 'cold', [kɔkɔˈɺɛkɔ] 'sweet potato', [ˌjɔkʊˈjɔkʊ] 'sweat').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: in words with reduplicated syllable pairs, secondary stress on the first syllable of the reduplicated pair ([ˌba.giˈba.gi] 'work'); transcriptions also show [ˌbɔnʊˈbɔnʊ] 'pumpkin', [ˌsimˈsim] 'watermelon', [ɺɔˌfɐɺɔˈfɐnɐ] 'long'.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'generally'; no explicit exception list. Example transcriptions show some vowel-sequence/diphthong words with final-looking stress ([nɐwɐˈɺɐi] 'moon', [ˈgʷɐi] 'laugh', [fɐiˈɔnɐ] 'three'), consistent with VV sequences counting as one syllable (CVV is a listed syllable type). Vowel length is absent in reduplicated syllables and two-vowel syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (citation forms in an SIL OPD wordlist; draft, unreviewed, 5 pp.). /u/ has [u] in stressed syllables, [ʊ] elsewhere (p. 4).
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD covers 'Kakabai Language [KQF]' as a whole (villages Mainawa, Kwabunaki, Takwatakwai, Boilavi); it notes dialectal variation only for /ɺ/ and /ɣ/ realizations, not for stress. Glottolog kaka1267 lists Igora as an alternate name (Ross 1988: 'Kakabai (= Igora)'); Lithgow 1976 treats Igora as a dialect of the Kakabai family. No separate glottocode for Igora.

sources.note: p. 3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': stress is predictable, generally on the penultimate syllable of a word, realized as high pitch + vowel lengthening; words with reduplicated syllable pairs carry primary stress on the penult and secondary stress on the first syllable of the reduplicated pair ([ˌba.giˈba.gi] 'work'); all example transcriptions pp. 2-3 mark stress (mostly penultimate; the few exceptions are diphthong/coda cases like [pɔʊ], [ˈgʷɐi], [nɐwɐˈɺɐi]).

sources.note: Sec. 84 'Stress' (p. 475) is a survey-wide note on the Papuan Tip Cluster: stress phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima; 'in all of the languages of PTC it seems that stress is predictable within certain word-classes, notably kinship nouns and verbs' (suffixation shifts stress one syllable rightward). Nothing specific to Kakabai; Kakabai sections 54 and 66 are lexicostatistics and morphology only.
